headline: Brazil hits historic low in Amazon deforestation
meta_description: Brazil's Amazon and Cerrado savanna reached their lowest deforestation rates ever recorded, with a 42% drop in the past year under President Lula's administrat…
summary_short: Brazil has achieved the lowest deforestation levels ever recorded in the Amazon rainforest and Cerrado savanna, marking a dramatic reversal from recent years.
body:
Brazil has achieved a milestone that scientists say marks a turning point for two of the world's most vital ecosystems. Between August 2025 and July 2026, deforestation in the Amazon fell to just 3,335 square kilometers—a 42% drop from the previous year and the lowest rate since satellite monitoring began in 1988. The Cerrado tropical savanna, another critical region, also hit its lowest deforestation level since measurements started in 2001, falling 24% to 5,516.69 square kilometers. These reductions occurred under incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, presenting a stark contrast to the spike in forest clearing that occurred under his predecessor.

The scale of the reversal becomes clear when looking back. In 2021, under far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, deforestation peaked at over 13,200 square kilometers—nearly four times the current rate. University of São Paulo climate scientist Carlos Nobre called the new figures "very positive," noting they represent the lowest deforestation in the Amazon since intensive clearing began during Brazil's military dictatorship in the mid-1970s. The three states historically responsible for the most forest loss—Pará, Mato Grosso, and Amazonas—all recorded steep declines, with each seeing drops above 45%.

Brazil's environment and climate change minister, João Paulo Capobianco, emphasized that this reduction was no accident. He attributed the sustained decline to using science to guide policy decisions and fostering cooperation between federal, state, and municipal governments. The achievement suggests that when political will aligns with coordinated action, even vast ecological systems can begin to recover. As Brazilians prepare for elections, these numbers show what's possible when forest protection becomes a genuine priority.

Lowest rate recorded since satellite monitoring began in 1988
Pará, Mato Grosso, and Amazonas each saw deforestation drop over 45%
2021 peak under Bolsonaro was 13,200 km²—nearly four times higher
Cerrado savanna also hit its lowest deforestation rate since 2001
